prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first. It meets the criterion I care most about: a discovery that opened a door to phenomena nobody could access before. A single twist angle turns a simple material into a tunable platform for flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity, and the 2018 transport experiments were the original observation, directly guided by a quantitative prediction (Bistritzer-MacDonald 2011) of where to look. That is rare: a number predicted, then found. The result has been reproduced in many independent laboratories since 2018 and has spread to other moire systems, so the central phenomena are experimentally verified, not just plausible. The dated historical record is also comparatively clean: the prediction (2011) and the discovery (2018) are unambiguous, and the structure of a theory-plus-experiment prize fits the three-person limit. Bistritzer should stay in the set because the continuum-model calculation that identified the magic angle is his and MacDonald's jointly, and the committee should be sure it has credited the people who did the original work.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is maturity and interpretation. The field is only eight years old, the microscopic origin of the superconductivity is unsettled, and twist-angle disorder and sample variability complicate reproducibility. The experimental credit is also awkward: the 2018 measurements were done by Yuan Cao, Valla Fatemi and colleagues in Jarillo-Herrero's group, who cannot be named under the three-person limit, and other groups (Dean, Young, Yacoby, Kim and others) contributed to the wider moire field in parallel. The discovery is verified, but the prize rule that the original experimenters be identified with certainty is harder to satisfy here than for a mature, instrument-led topic such as lattice clocks, and I must test my own enthusiasm for the platform against this.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect first, and sees twisted bilayer graphene as only about eight years old, perhaps somewhat premature, with the superconducting mechanism unsettled; he would credit only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero.
responses.response: I accept the maturity concern but not that it is decisive: the Prize requires an experimentally verified discovery, and the existence of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle has been reproduced widely, whereas the pairing mechanism is a follow-up question that does not change what was discovered. On the two-name version, I disagree. Bistritzer and MacDonald produced the flat-band prediction jointly, and dropping Bistritzer would leave out a person who did part of the original work, which is exactly what I want to avoid. I also hold a serious qualification about B012: three names cannot represent the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal that Molenkamp's experiment tested, nor the 3D work, and Zhang has died. The credit problem there looks harder to repair than the one for B047.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first on the strength of strong coupling on a chip and its follow-on from the 2025 prize, and ranks twisted bilayer graphene third, noting that the superconductivity mechanism is debated and sample-to-sample variability complicates reproducibility.
responses.response: I agree that reproducibility needs honest treatment: twist-angle disorder makes individual devices vary. Still, the phenomenology appears across many groups, which is the relevant test for a discovery. On circuit QED, I would qualify rather than reject. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is close enough that a second circuit prize so soon looks heavy, and I would want to hear whether the committee can separate the strong-coupling discovery from the transmon and architecture work of Yale colleagues who are not among Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf. Your own caveat about knowing these groups is a fair point to weigh.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a new measurement capability, with a clean Katori and Ye pair, strong independent confirmation, and a pending redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I share your preference for new instruments that open doors, and lattice clocks are my own fourth choice and my first alternative. The attribution is cleaner than in nearly any other candidate. My reservations are narrower: the societal payoff through the redefinition of the second is still in progress, and relative to the 2005 comb prize and the ion-clock prize I want the committee to be sure that the lattice-clock idea (Katori's magic wavelength) is the original discovery rather than a refinement of earlier metrology. If we settle that, I would not oppose B019, but I would still place the broader scientific opening for new physics with the moire platform.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks twisted bilayer graphene second and values the clean prediction-and-experiment pairing and reproduction across groups, while acknowledging that Cao is not among the credited names and that some members may prefer to wait.
responses.response: I agree with you on the pairing and on the three-name configuration. I would add that the omission of Cao and Fatemi is the one point where I want the record checked most carefully, because the experiment is the part of the story I give most weight. I do not think waiting is neutral: the evidence is already in and independent confirmation exists, so delay mainly risks the attribution becoming harder to sort out as the field grows. On your first-place choice of active matter, I would ask whether it is a single decisive experimentally verified discovery, given that quantitative tests of the Toner-Tu exponents are limited and Yuhai Tu is missing from the names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can justify naming Jarillo-Herrero alone on the experimental side when Cao, Fatemi and other 2018 coauthors did the measurements.
Whether the unsettled pairing mechanism makes the prize premature or only leaves a follow-up question.
Whether the 2018 experimental priority needs checking against parallel moire work and earlier twist-angle studies.
Whether lattice clocks (B019) are an original discovery or a later refinement relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile with any shortlisted candidate or credited name. My profile lists frequent co-authors and mentors, none of whom are among them. I note only that Goran Johansson is also at Chalmers Physics and Mehlig is at the neighbouring Gothenburg University department, which does not bear on these candidates.
